hints.junior: A pricing card three components deep stayed white-on-white in dark mode — the override that would've fixed it targeted a different class name.
hints.mid: 40-plus dark-mode override rules scattered across a dozen files, and nobody could say for sure they covered every component.
hints.staff: The real defect was treating color as a per-component detail instead of a themeable value with one source of truth — that burden compounds with every component and every theme.

hints.junior: Toggle dark mode, then add a card in each panel — watch what happens to the new card's colors.
hints.mid: Broken mode's new card ships hardcoded and needs its own override. Token mode's new card already themes correctly with zero extra code.
hints.staff: Broken mode's override count grows with every component added. Token mode's stays flat at 'redefine 5 tokens once.'

hints.junior: Name the color by what it's for, not what it looks like — --color-surface instead of a hex value — then redefine it once per theme at the root.
hints.mid: Every component references the token, never a raw value, so a theme is just a different value block for the same token names.
hints.staff: This moves the theming decision from 'asked separately for every component' to 'asked once at the root' — the same cascade mechanism that already scales CSS, applied to color.

hints.junior: Name tokens by role (--color-surface), not appearance (--color-gray-100) — a role survives a theme changing what it looks like.
hints.mid: A two-layer system — primitive values aliased to semantic roles — lets a theme remap which primitive backs a token without renaming what components depend on.
hints.staff: A component reading a token via getComputedStyle in JS needs to re-read it on theme change — JS doesn't get cascade updates the way CSS declarations do.

sections.junior: A team added dark mode the fast way, component by component, override by override. Three weeks in, a pricing card buried a few levels deep was still white on white, because the override that would've caught it targeted a totally different class name.
sections.mid: By then there were over 40 dark-mode override rules scattered across a dozen files, and nobody could say with confidence they actually covered every component.
sections.staff: The real problem wasn't the missing override, it was treating color as a per-component detail instead of a themeable value with one source of truth.

sections.junior: A design token names what a color is for, not what it looks like — surface instead of white, ink instead of near-black. Components reference the token, and a theme just redefines it once at the root.
sections.mid: Switching themes becomes swapping which value block is active. Every component that already referenced the token updates automatically, with zero component code changed.
sections.staff: This flips where the theming decision lives — instead of asking 'what should this look like in dark mode' once per component, you ask it exactly once, at the root, and the cascade does the rest.

sections.junior: Toggle dark mode in each panel, then add a new card, and watch what happens to its colors.
sections.mid: The hardcoded panel's new card needs its own override to look right. The token panel's new card already themes correctly, no extra code at all.
sections.staff: Notice the cost curve — the override panel grows with every component you add, the token panel stays flat no matter how many components exist.

sections.junior: Hardcoded colors plus reactive overrides never stop growing. Name colors by role and redefine them once per theme instead.
sections.mid: Reference the token everywhere, redefine the token set once at the root per theme, and components need zero changes to support a new one.
sections.staff: A two-layer token system scales further, but the real win is structural — the theming decision moves from per-component to once, at the root.
